Task: run an impeccable-style design pass on the account, connection and first-run experience of Email OS (Vue 3 + Tauri desktop email client), then implement the fixes. Context: a UI/UX review of the whole app scored this area 22/40 heuristics, attention 8/10 (the highest, tied with reader/compose, which has since shipped). The review was done from code only (nothing rendered), so VERIFY each finding by reading the code/tests (and reproducing it in a test) before fixing; if one is wrong, say so and skip it. Read PRODUCT.md and DESIGN.md first (brand: focused, precise, trustworthy; keyboard-first; honest state over smooth feel; anti-references: Gmail clutter, generic SaaS cards, optimistic UI that lies; voice is terse and factual). See .impeccable/critique/*.md for the critique format. Recent merged work you should reuse patterns from (compact rows, one-line honest status, Seam underline inputs, ghost buttons): the reader/compose PRs (#29 and the follow-up). Another thread is concurrently reworking the Activity/Drafts/Reminders/Cached Trash drawer panels (branch impeccable/drawer-panels) and may introduce a shared drawer-row pattern and drawer spacing; keep your changes to AccountPanel and ProviderDestinations self-contained and, where you need drawer chrome, follow whatever is already on main rather than redesigning it. Do not touch those four panels. Files in scope: src/components/AccountPanel.vue, ProviderDestinations.vue, src/FixtureWorkspaces.vue, the App.vue paths for first launch / no account, connect Gmail, OAuth in progress, permission upgrade (gmail.modify), initial sync/loading, sync failure, offline, disconnect, account switching (grep accountReady, accountStatus, switchAccountLabel, gmailMode, sync, 'Determining account mode'), the header note slot (.header-note, read-only hint, ~App.vue 2218), the empty-inbox state (~App.vue 2473), their CSS in src/assets/style.css (account ~1863-1920, workspace header ~187), and tests (account.component, provider-destinations.*, workspaces.component, app.component). Findings to verify and address, in priority order: 1. P0 False empty state. App.vue ~2473 shows "No conversations are currently in the inbox. Archived conversations stay recoverable from Activity." for not_configured, disconnected, auth_required and during initial sync; none of that is true then, and there is no Connect action. Branch the empty state on connection/sync status with one terse honest line and an inline action: e.g. "Not connected. Connect Gmail", "Sign-in expired. Sign in again", "Syncing first mail… N cached", "Sync failed. Retry". Keep the real "inbox is empty" text only for a genuinely synced, connected, empty inbox. 2. P0 Reachability. The Account rail entry appears only when gmailMode && accountStatus (~App.vue 2300); verify whether a user with no account can reach Connect in every mode (native Gmail profile before any account exists, fixture, browser preview). If not, fix it; tests currently only cover it once gmail() is mocked. If verified fine, say so. 3. P1 No global status. Sync running, sync error, offline, auth_required and connecting are invisible outside the Account drawer (grep sync.state in App.vue finds nothing). Extend the existing header note slot into one status slot using the same pattern as the read-only hint and "Review access": "Syncing…", "Sync failed · Retry", "Sign-in expired · Sign in", offline, with the cached count. Honest wording about what works meanwhile ("Reading works; actions off"). 4. P1 AccountPanel (~65-82, 108-139, 154-157): initial sync is one sentence with no progress; coverageText is long; a permanent "Disposable test account." note and the full disconnect warning are always shown with equal weight so the real action is lost. Make Disconnect an inline confirm that reveals the warning only then; remove the permanent disposable note (move to a title or settings detail if still needed); when mutationAccess is 'upgrading'/authenticating show "Finish sign-in in your browser" with Cancel as primary; put Retry inline next to the sync-error message. 5. P1 ProviderDestinations.vue: bare

/
I'll start by reading the product docs, critique format, and relevant code.

1	# Product
2	
3	## Register
4	
5	product
6	
7	## Users
8	
9	Initially a single person: the author, dogfooding a single-account desktop client (macOS first) against their own Gmail inbox in focused, keyboard-first sessions. They move through a high volume of mail quickly, want to reach "done" on each conversation, and need to trust that every action (archive, bulk processing, undo, send) did exactly what it claimed. The provider's own client remains the fallback.
10	
11	Longer term: technically capable people who want to compose their own email workflow (custom views, triage signals, commands, automations), manually or with an agent, without rebuilding sync, credentials, or send safety.
12	
13	The primary task on most screens is triage: scan the list, open a conversation, decide, act, move on.
14	
15	## Product Purpose
16	
17	A composable email client: a trusted mail engine (sync, safe rendering, credentials, action execution) with replaceable signals, views, commands, and workflows on top. It ships an opinionated reference experience, a compact Superhuman-style browsing and keyboard flow, rather than a blank toolkit.
18	
19	The near-term goal is a complete, trustworthy inbox-processing session. Strategic scope is set by `docs/adr/0001-single-account-desktop-email-client.md` and `superhuman-email-browsing-ux-spec.md`; this file does not expand it.
20	
21	Success looks like: the author processes their inbox faster and with more confidence than in their previous client, and every automated or bulk action is previewable, reported honestly (including partial success and "outcome unknown"), and undoable where undo is real.
22	
23	## Brand Personality
24	
25	**Focused, precise, trustworthy.**
26	
27	- **Focused:** the interface recedes so the mail and the next decision are what's on screen. Dense, quiet, few competing elements.
28	- **Precise:** exact states, exact counts, exact wording. No vague "something went wrong", no rounded-off truth about what happened.
29	- **Trustworthy:** the client never overstates what it did. Pending, failed, partial, and ambiguous outcomes are visible and distinct. Automation shows its work before it acts.
30	
31	Voice is terse and factual: short labels, plain verbs, no exclamation marks, no cheerleading.
32	
33	## Anti-references
34	
35	- **Gmail-web clutter:** toolbars of rarely-used icons, chrome competing with content, permanent competing panels.
36	- **"AI magic" email products:** AI destinations, sparkle icons, generated summaries presented as fact, fabricated contact enrichment, automation that acts without a preview.
37	- **Superhuman feature-parity clone:** Superhuman is the visual and interaction reference for browsing (layout, density, type, keyboard feel), and close look parity there is a goal. Features and workflows are our own; don't import Superhuman's product scope or claim verified behavioral parity.
38	- **Generic SaaS dashboard aesthetics:** card stacks and grids, gradient heroes, oversized rounded panels, decorative illustration or motion.
39	- **Optimistic UI that lies:** "Done" before the provider confirmed, silent retries of ambiguous sends, dead controls that look actionable.
40	
41	## Design Principles
42	
43	1. **Honest state over smooth feel.** When speed and truthfulness conflict, show the truth. Every action has a visible pending, success, partial, failed, or unknown state. Show evidence and coverage, including unknown and retained facts.
44	2. **Keyboard first, mouse welcome.** Every core triage path is reachable and discoverable from the keyboard; pointer interaction is supported, never required.
45	3. **Content is the interface.** Chrome stays quiet and compact so the list and the conversation dominate. Add UI only when it earns its space in the triage loop; reuse established commands, navigation and recovery surfaces before adding new ones.
46	4. **Preview before power.** Bulk actions, automations, and agent-proposed changes show what they will do before they do it, and report exactly what they did after. Focus, bulk selection and message identity stay separate concepts.
47	5. **Opinionated defaults, replaceable parts.** Ship one strong way of working; design surfaces so views, signals, and commands can be swapped without breaking the core experience.
48	
49	Standing constraints: ordinary reading stays local and non-mutating; message content renders as safe literal plain text; drafts stay local-only.
50	
51	## Accessibility & Inclusion
52	
53	Not a formal priority at this stage; no WCAG conformance target or certification is implied. Keyboard operability and visible focus remain required because they are core to the keyboard-first model. Don't regress behavior that already exists (explicit action labels, editable/IME shortcut protection, reduced-motion alternatives, selection/outcome announcements). The existing desktop/contact breakpoints remain authoritative; no new mobile UI. Revisit if the audience expands beyond the author.
54

163	# Design System: Email OS
164	
165	## 1. Overview
166	
167	**Creative North Star: "The Quiet Instrument"**
168	
169	A precision tool used in long, focused sessions. The surface is a single warm charcoal plane. The interface recedes until only the list, the open conversation and the next decision are on screen. Density is high but calm: 36px rows, small type, no dividers, no cards. One violet signal marks where you are. Everything else is a tonal step on the same warm gray ramp.
170	
171	The system follows Superhuman's browsing look closely, and that parity is an explicit goal. It covers geometry, density, type scale, tonal layering and the focused-row treatment. Features and workflows stay our own. The one place we deliberately go our own way is state: pending, failed, partial and outcome-unknown states are always visible in their own form (*"Honest state over smooth feel"*, PRODUCT.md). A quiet surface must never hide what happened.
172	
173	The system rejects Gmail-web clutter, "AI magic" sparkle chrome, generic SaaS dashboards (card grids, gradient heroes, oversized rounded panels), and optimistic UI that says "Done" before the provider confirms.
174	
175	**Key Characteristics:**
176	- Three fixed panes: a 40px icon rail, a fluid list or reader, and a 272px darker contact pane. Each is separated by a single 1px divider.
177	- One content inset (50px from the list pane's left edge). It aligns split tabs, sender names, date-group captions, notices, banners and the bottom dock.
178	- 36px rows on 12px type. Hierarchy comes from weight and tone, not size.
179	- Pane-edge alignment: the contact name sits on the split-tab line, and the contact email sits on the first-row line.
180	- Flat tonal layering. No shadows in the browsing shell.
181	- The violet accent appears once per screen: on the focused row or the active message.
182	
183	**Layout geometry (approximate calibration targets).** These values come from the 2026-11-07 Superhuman reference capture (1603×2000 image px). The capture was scaled by about 1.56 image px per CSS px, calibrated from the macOS traffic-light pitch of 20pt and cross-checked against the 36px rhythm and the 40px and 270px pane widths in `superhuman-email-browsing-ux-spec.md`. Verify them on real displays.
184	- **Rail:** 40px wide. The top action button (28px circle) is centered on the split-tab line (42px down). The navigation icons sit in a dark pill about 30px wide that starts near the header's bottom edge, with its first glyph centered on the first list line (96px down) and a 28px pitch. The active glyph sits on a 24px Rail Pebble disc inside the pill.
185	- **Split header:** 78px from the content top to the first row. Tabs are vertically centered about 42px down. The hamburger is centered 23px into the pane. Tabs start at the 50px content inset with an 18px gap; the count sits 4px after its label. Compose and search icons are right-aligned on the 32px action pitch.
186	- **Rows:** 36px. The highlight is inset 6px from both pane edges. There is a 44px left gutter, with the 5px unread dot centered about 34px into the row. The sender column is 132px, and subject→snippet→meta gaps are 12px. The trailing date sits about 25px from the pane edge. On focus, three 16px action glyphs replace the date at a 32px pitch.
187	- **Date groups:** a 48px block, with the caption vertically centered on the content inset.
188	- **Contact pane:** 272px with a 24px inner inset. The name is centered on the tab line (42px), the email on the first list line (96px), the "Mail" label about 36px lower (~131px) and the first thread at ~156px, then a 24px pitch. Superhuman's footer toolbar sits 24px from the bottom: a ghost label plus 16px glyphs at a 28px pitch.
189	
190	### Parity Gaps (current code → target)
191	
192	This is the backlog for layout, typeset and polish passes. Each gap names what ships today and what this spec requires.
193	
194	1. **Split header.** Done (2026-11-07 header pass). The header is one borderless 78px strip inside the list column (the rail and contact pane span its height). It has a Graphite hamburger (Destinations navigator) centered 23px in, split tabs on the 50px inset (16px, active Paper White, inactive Smoke, 11px Ash count 4px after the label, 18px apart), and right-hand glyphs on the 32px pitch: Back (when there is history), Reminders (fixture only), the Starred-only toggle, Commands and Search. There is no brand text, no visible h1 while a tab is active, and no bordered chips. Glyphs are local inline SVG (`HeaderGlyph.vue`).
195	   - The context h1 stays in the accessibility tree. It is shown on screen, styled like an active tab, only when no rendered tab is active (Cached Done, Starred, Search, the reader, an open drawer).
196	   - The status line is removed. The inbox count is on the active tab; loaded counts were dropped as duplicates of the list. Selection count stays in SelectionBar, plus a visually hidden polite announcement. The pending count is covered by row "Pending…", the action notice and Activity. The Shift+U hint is in the Commands palette. The command error is its own alert line beside the action notice in the list column's bottom dock (gap 13). The read-only hint and the Unread-only/Starred-only filter states stay visible in words in the header.
197	   - The Inbox coverage sentence is the tabs' accessible description and the tab strip's hover title. The browser-preview banner is a one-line amber "Preview · in-memory" note on the right; the full disclosure is its title and accessible text.
198	   - Utility drawers now start below the header, so they never cover its glyphs.
199	   Update: the compose glyph now ships. It sits on the right of the header, left of Search, as a Graphite glyph on the 32px pitch, and opens the local-draft compose card INLINE in the central pane ("New Message", C key / palette action "Compose new local draft") — an in-flow card that replaces the list while composing, not a modal overlay: no backdrop and no dimming, so the rail, header and contact pane stay visible. (While a reader is open, the card docks at the bottom of the reader pane, like the reply composer.) There is still no compose capability beyond local drafts, so the glyph opens the local-only inline card, never a sender. (The aggregate pending count now lives on the Activity rail badge, and the tab line is calibrated against the rail's home circle: both are centered 42px down; see gap 2.)
200	2. **Rail.** Done (2026-11-07 rail/contact layout pass). The rail is a fixed 40px column (px, so larger root fonts widen the list, never the rail) with a 1px Seam on its right.
201	   - **Home circle:** Inbox is the 28px Rail Pebble circle, centered on the split-tab line. We have no AI or compose action to put there, so the primary destination takes the slot instead of an empty or dead control.
202	   - **Inkwell pill:** a 30px pill (the capture measures ~30px, not 28px) holds Starred (Gmail), Cached Done, Provider mail and Cached Trash (Gmail) as 16px glyphs on 28px hit targets at a 28px pitch. Its first glyph is centered on the first list line.
203	   - **Utilities:** Account (Gmail), Activity, Drafts and the narrow-viewport Contact disclosure are ghost glyphs at the bottom, 16px from the edge.
204	   - **States:** the current destination (`aria-current`) or open drawer (`aria-expanded`) shows a Paper White glyph on a 24px Rail Pebble disc; the rest are Graphite and rise to Paper White on hover and focus.
205	   - **Labels:** every button keeps its text label as its accessible name (a visually hidden span, so `textContent` is unchanged), its hover `title` (the action label with its shortcut, as on the header glyphs), and a keyboard tooltip: the same label shown beside the rail on `:focus-visible`, with Popover lift.
206	   - **Activity badge:** a small Amber Notice count on the Activity glyph shows unresolved operations, i.e. `queued`/`applying` plus `outcome_unknown`. It is derived from the activity rows the drawer already lists, with no new read. The digit is `aria-hidden`; the words ("2 operations pending", "1 operation with outcome unknown", or "3 operations unresolved: 2 pending, 1 outcome unknown") are the button's `aria-describedby` and are appended to its title. The badge disappears at zero.
207	   - **Glyphs:** local inline SVG in `PaneGlyph.vue` (Starred reuses HeaderGlyph's star). The rail sits at z-index 20 (above the row popover at 6, below drawers at 30).
208	   Remaining: the badge counts only what the activity snapshot carries (the same rows Activity shows), not a separate mailbox-wide total. The Contact disclosure stays in the rail below 1000px; it has no Superhuman analogue.
209	3. **Row metrics.** Done (2026-11-07 rows pass): 12px type in two weights, a fixed 36px height, no per-row dividers, the 6px pane inset, the 44px left gutter and the 132px sender column. Leading caption: done (polish pass). When the list opens with Today, that caption is visually hidden (it stays in the accessibility tree), so the first row is centered on the 96px first-list line with the rail's first glyph and the contact email, as in the reference. Today's rows already show a time, so nothing is lost on screen. Any other leading bucket (Yesterday, Earlier this month, a month, Unknown date) stays visible, because a list that starts in the past must say where it starts; in that case the first row is still centered 144px down.
210	4. **Focused row.** Done (rows pass): the fill is inset 6px from both pane edges, with a 4px Dusk Lavender bar on its own left edge.
211	5. **Read state.** Done (rows pass): a 5px `unread-marker` dot in the gutter, a distinct hollow ring when read state is unknown, and read senders drop to weight 400.
212	6. **Selection checkbox.** Done (rows pass): hidden until selection mode, hover or focus, and placed in the 44px gutter.
213	7. **Row actions.** Done (rows pass): `icon-muted` inline SVG glyphs (`RowGlyph.vue`) replace the date on the focused or hovered row only. Accessible names, roving tab stops and the `meta-compact` disclosure stay. The disclosure now also re-measures on text-size changes inside an unchanged row box (rail/contact pass: the sender label is observed too). Remaining: Superhuman shows done/snooze/more; we show only our real actions (read/unread, done).
214	8. **Date-group caption.** Done (rows pass): title case, 12px `text-secondary`, a 48px block, no rule, on the content inset. A leading Today caption is visually hidden (gap 3).
215	9. **Contact pane.** Done (2026-11-07 rail/contact layout pass; type from the typeset pass). A fixed 272px column on Deep Umber with a `0 24px 24px` inset.
216	   - **No visible caption:** the "Focused conversation" / "Open conversation" h2 stays in the accessibility tree (visually hidden).
217	   - **Pinned lines:** the name (16px regular Headline) is centered on the tab line at 42px and wraps around that center before it moves anything. The email (12px semibold Title) is centered on the first list line at 96px.
218	   - **Copy controls:** each copy control is a 16px Graphite glyph in the trailing slot of its own line, revealed by opacity on line hover or focus. It stays focusable, and it no longer leaves an empty line when hidden. Without a display name, Copy email moves to the name line.
219	   - **Recent cached mail:** a Title label with a 16px envelope glyph (~129px), then plain Ash text rows at a 24px pitch (first at 156px). Each row has an ellipsis and the full subject as its title, rises to Paper White on hover or focus, and is still a button.
220	   - **Narrow disclosure:** inside the Contact disclosure below 1000px, the same content stacks compactly under the drawer header.
221	   - **No footer toolbar:** Account, Activity and Drafts stay in the rail, their one home. The contact column does not exist below 1000px and is `inert` while a drawer is open, so footer toggles would vanish on narrow viewports and could not close their own drawer or receive focus back.
222	   Remaining: the label keeps our honest copy "Recent cached mail" rather than "Mail" (vocabulary pass). The list is still the 4 most recent cached results from the sender search, not a provider-complete thread list.
223	10. **Palette deltas.** Done: `text-primary` #ece9e2 → #ffffff (typeset pass), `text-secondary` #a8a29a → #c0bcb6 (rows pass), `text-tertiary`, `icon-muted` and `unread-marker` added (header and rows passes), the undefined `--text-muted` on coverage notes now maps to `text-secondary`, and `rail-well` / `rail-button` are CSS tokens (rail pass). `divider` is now #474543 (polish pass): the rail and contact-pane seams, the drawer's leading edge, utility-chip and input borders, the compact row-actions popover and the command-overlay hint rule. It never separates rows (the list has no row borders). The old #3b3936 survives as the quieter `rule` token for structure inside a pane, only in the reader (toolbar and message rules) and inside drawers (Activity and draft rows, group detail, Account panel, Reminders fieldset), so those surfaces keep their tone until a reader reference is captured. `focus-accent` stays at the committed #bba5ed; the capture reads about #bfa1f6, which is within capture and color-profile noise.
224	11. **Global button style.** Done (polish pass). The `button` defaults are zero-specificity (`:where()`), so every component class keeps its own look. The default is a ghost: transparent, Paper White, 4px radius, `4px 8px` (24px tall at 12px, the old chip's hit target), Lifted Charcoal on hover, Focus Stone on press, 0.45 opacity when disabled, and the 2px Dusk Lavender focus ring at a 1px offset. 241	## 2. Colors
242	
243	One warm charcoal ramp, one violet signal, and two status hues reserved for truth-telling.
244	
245	### Primary
246	- **Dusk Lavender** (`focus-accent`): the single "you are here" signal. Used for the 4px bar on the focused row, the active message bar in the reader, focus outlines, and the highlighted command. It never fills an area and never decorates.
247	
248	### Secondary
249	- **Orchid Dot** (`unread-marker`): only for the 5px unread dot in the row gutter. It is pinker than Dusk Lavender so that unread and focus never read as the same signal.
250	
251	### Neutral
252	- **Warm Charcoal** (`surface`): the list, rail and header plane. Everything sits on it.
253	- **Deep Umber** (`surface-contact`): the contact pane and utility drawers. It is one step darker, so context reads as secondary to the list.
254	- **Lifted Charcoal** (`surface-raised`): utility chips, overlays and inputs.
255	- **Focus Stone** (`focus-fill`): the focused-row and active-message fill, and the highlighted command item.
256	- **Inkwell** (`rail-well`): the pill behind the rail's navigation glyphs.
257	- **Rail Pebble** (`rail-button`): the circular rail action button.
258	- **Paper White** (`text-primary`): sender, subject, active tab, contact name and email, labels.
259	- **Ash** (`text-secondary`): snippet, date, group caption, contact threads, counts.
260	- **Smoke** (`text-tertiary`): inactive split tabs.
261	- **Graphite** (`icon-muted`): every resting glyph (row actions, compose, search, hamburger, footer icons, attachment). Hover and focus raise glyphs to Paper White. Graphite is 2.75:1 on Focus Stone and 3.79:1 on Lifted Charcoal, so it never carries meaningful text, or a glyph that must be read, on a focus fill or the composer fill; Ash does that job there.
262	- **Seam** (`divider`): the 1px vertical separators between rail, list and contact pane, and the drawer's leading edge; also the 1px border of utility chips, fields and floating panels. Never between rows.
263	- **Rule** (`rule`): a quieter 1px structure line inside a pane, used only in the reader and inside drawers. Never in the list.
264	
265	### Status
266	- **Amber Notice** (`warning`): pending, outcome unknown, local-only, expired-undo and partial states.
267	- **Coral Fault** (`danger`): confirmed failures and command errors.
268	
269	### Named Rules
270	**The One Signal Rule.** Dusk Lavender appears at most once per screen, on the current row or message. If two violet things are visible, one of them is wrong.
271	
272	**The Seams-Only Rule.** Dividers separate panes, never rows. Rows are separated by rhythm alone.
273	
274	**The Status-Is-Sacred Rule.** Amber and coral are never used decoratively, and a status is never shown only as a tint: every status carries words.

276	## 3. Typography
277	
278	**Body Font:** system-ui (with -apple-system, sans-serif)
279	**Label/Mono Font:** ui-monospace, for plain-text message bodies only
280	
281	**Character:** One local system sans in two weights carries the whole UI. Hierarchy comes from weight (600 vs 400) and tone (Paper White vs Ash), not size. The browsing shell uses just two sizes.
282	
283	### Hierarchy
284	- **Headline** (400, 1rem / 16px, 1.25): split tabs and the contact name. This is the only large text in the shell.
285	- **Title** (600, 0.75rem / 12px, 1.35): sender names, contact email, section labels ("Mail"), footer labels, notice labels.
286	- **Body** (400, 0.75rem / 12px, 1.35): subject (Paper White), snippet and threads (Ash), date-group captions (Ash).
287	- **Label** (400, 0.75rem / 12px, tabular numerals): dates ("8:00 AM", "6 NOV" with an uppercase month) and counts in status text.
288	- **Mono** and the other steps are CSS tokens: `--type-headline`, `--type-body`, `--type-count`, `--type-mono`, `--weight-regular`, `--weight-strong` (`src/assets/style.css`). Use the tokens, never a literal size.
289	
290	### Dates
291	Row and reader dates are one fixed product format, not a locale format. They depend only on the instant, the current time and the viewer's time zone (`src/lib/browsing-dates.ts`). Month group captions ("October 2026") still follow the locale.
292	- **Row, today:** the time, 12-hour, no leading zero: "8:00 AM", "12:05 PM".
293	- **Row, earlier this calendar year:** day and month: "6 NOV". The DOM text is "6 Nov"; CSS uppercases it, so screen readers hear a word, not letters.
294	- **Row, any other year (past or future):** day, month and four-digit year: "9 JAN 2025". The day is kept for precision, and a two-digit year would read as another day.
295	- **Unknown or unparsable:** "Unknown" in the row, "Unknown date" in full form. Never blank.
296	- **Full form** (reader message times, the row date's hover title): "Thu 9 Jan 2025, 6:29 PM". The same 12-hour clock as the row.
297	- Every rendered date is a `<time>` with a normalized ISO `datetime` when the timestamp parses.
298	- **Count** (400, 0.6875rem / 11px): split-tab counts, set 4px after the tab label.
299	- **Mono** (400, 0.85rem, 1.45): the current plain-text message body in the reader.
300	
301	Sizes are rem so the 16px and 20px root-font layouts in `tests/inbox-list.rendered-layout.test.ts` still scale. Row and header heights are min-heights in px. The 12px row size is measured from the capture: system-ui glyph metrics point to 11.5–12px.
302	
303	### Named Rules
304	**The Two-Size Rule.** The browsing shell uses 16px and 12px only (11px for counts). A third size in the list needs a written reason.
305	
306	**The No-Caps-Caption Rule.** No uppercase letter-spaced captions in the browsing shell. Date groups and pane headings are title case. Uppercase is allowed only for the month in compact dates.

309	
310	The browsing shell is flat. Depth comes from tonal layering: Warm Charcoal for the plane, Deep Umber for context, Focus Stone for the current row, Inkwell for the rail well. No shadows sit on rows, panes, the header or the rail. Shadows appear only on surfaces that truly float above the shell and cover it.

312	### Shadow Vocabulary
313	- **Drawer cast** (`box-shadow: -8px 0 24px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.35)`): the right-edge utility drawer (Activity, Account, Drafts).
314	- **Popover lift** (`box-shadow: 0 6px 16px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.35)`): the compact row-actions disclosure panel.
315	- **Overlay lift** (`box-shadow: 0 16px 64px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.53)`): the command palette and navigator, over a `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.53)` backdrop (`--overlay-lift`, `--overlay-backdrop`).
316	
317	### Named Rules
318	**The Flat-Shell Rule.** If something in the rail, header, list or contact pane casts a shadow, remove it. Shadows mean "this covers the shell", nothing else.

375	### In-flow Notices (Action notice, Selection bar, coverage and recovery)
376	- **Style:** borderless lines in normal flow, with text on the 50px content inset, in Body type with 6px block padding. Status words use Amber Notice or Coral Fault. Undo shows its `kbd` hint in Ash. They never overlay rows and never auto-hide a failure.
377	- **Bottom dock (transient lines):** the Selection bar, the Action notice and the command-error alert sit in a dock at the bottom of the list column, below the list, never above it. Showing or hiding them never moves a row. The dock reserves one 36px line and grows upward into the list viewport; the focused row is kept whole when the viewport shrinks. Its lines are whole-pixel (16px line height, 24px buttons). This is the honest, in-flow form of Superhuman's bottom undo toast: no float, no shadow, nothing covered.
378	- **Above the list (static lines):** Starred/Done coverage notes and the draft-close recovery banner, which belong to the destination or to a pending recovery rather than to the last keystroke.
379	
380	## 6. Do's and Don'ts
381	
382	### Do:
383	- **Do** keep rows at exactly 36px with 12px type, and separate them by rhythm alone.
384	- **Do** align split tabs, sender names, date captions, notices and the bottom dock to the single 50px content inset.
385	- **Do** use Dusk Lavender (#bba5ed) only for the current row or message, and the focus ring.
386	- **Do** show every pending, partial, failed and outcome-unknown state in words, in Amber Notice or Coral Fault, where the user is already looking.
387	- **Do** align the contact pane to the list: the name on the tab line, the email on the first-row line.
388	- **Do** ship glyphs as local inline SVG with an accessible name. No icon fonts and no CDN.
389	- **Do** name each action once, in sentence case, on every surface (row glyph, selection bar, reader, Activity, action notice, palette): "Mark done" / "Mark not done" (E / Shift+E), "Mark read" / "Mark unread", "Star" / "Unstar". Counted forms keep the verb: "Mark 3 done". Destinations keep their proper names (Inbox, Done, Starred, Trash, Provider mail, Activity) after "Go to". "Archive" is the provider-side effect, never a label; it survives only as a palette search alias.
390	- **Do** treat Superhuman's browsing look as the visual and interaction reference. Close look parity is the goal (PRODUCT.md).
391	
392	### Don't:
393	- **Don't** draw dividers between rows or under the header. Seams separate panes only.
394	- **Don't** use uppercase letter-spaced captions in the browsing shell.
395	- **Don't** add Gmail-web clutter: toolbars of rarely-used icons, or chrome competing with content.
396	- **Don't** add "AI magic" chrome: sparkle icons, or generated summaries presented as fact.
397	- **Don't** build a Superhuman feature-parity clone. Copy the browsing look, not Superhuman's product scope.
398	- **Don't** use generic SaaS dashboard aesthetics: card grids, gradient heroes, oversized rounded panels, decorative illustration.
399	- **Don't** show optimistic UI that lies: no "Done" toast before the provider confirms, and no silent retry of an ambiguous send.
400	- **Don't** put shadows on anything in the rail, header, list or contact pane.
401	- **Don't** use Graphite for text or meaningful glyphs on Focus Stone or on the composer's Lifted Charcoal fill. Use Ash.
402	- **Don't** repeat a standing guarantee as a paragraph on every open. State it once, in a status line with the detail in its title; only exceptions interrupt.
403	- **Don't** introduce a third type size in the list, or use off-palette hex values (the old command-overlay violets are the cautionary example).
404	- **Don't** load remote fonts, images or CDN assets.

# Implement

Implement the requested change in Email OS. The request can be a task description, an approved plan, or a path to a repository document with a specific item to implement. No ticket service is required.

Usage: `/skill:implement <task description or document path and item>`

All repository paths below are relative to the repository root. The local persona definition is `.pi/agents/persona-feature-engineer.md` from the repository root. Runtimes that mirror these documents through symlinks keep this path authoritative; follow the target, not the mirror location.

## 1. Establish the task

- Read the request and referenced documents. Identify the goal, acceptance criteria, non-goals, and affected code.
- If the request names a broad document, ask which item to implement. Do not treat every proposed feature in that document as approved work.
- Ask for clarification if a product, architecture, data migration, or scope decision is missing. Do not invent requirements.
- Inspect the working-tree status. Preserve pre-existing edits and keep one writer per checkout.

## 2. Gather repository context

Use local code and documentation, not external wiki or code-graph services:

- `README.md` for the project entry points and document map.
- `docs/development.md` for setup, commands, profile isolation, and validation gates.
- `docs/adr/0001-single-account-desktop-email-client.md` for accepted first-build scope.
- The relevant slice or UX contract under `docs/`, and the relevant section of `docs/superhuman-browsing-implementation-plan.md` or `superhuman-email-browsing-ux-spec.md` for browsing work.
- `ARCHITECTURE.md` only as a proposal, not as an inventory of implemented behavior. The PRD and older research do not authorize scope expansion.
- Current code and tests to confirm actual behavior. Escalate material conflicts between the task, accepted contracts, and implementation.

Find the affected seam:

- `crates/mail-core/`: Rust mail core, DTOs, SQLite, Gmail auth/provider/cache/sync/actions.
- `src/` and `tests/`: Vue 3/TypeScript UI, IPC adapter, and frontend tests.
- `src-tauri/`: thin Tauri 2 native shell and command/event bridge.
- `src/lib/ipc/generated.ts`: generated wire contract. Never edit it by hand; change the Rust DTOs and run `mise run gen:ts`.

Follow existing conventions and any applicable project instructions. Do not invent a separate coding-standard source.

## 3. Delegate implementation

Using this skill authorizes one implementation subagent. Do not ask the user to request delegation again.

- Read your runtime's subagent guidance and the local persona definition before launch.
- Launch `persona-feature-engineer` with whatever subagent or delegation mechanism your own runtime provides (a native subagent tool, a task tool, a delegate API — the choice is yours and not prescribed here). Inherit the parent model unless the user specifies another one.
- Give the child a self-contained brief: explicit repository cwd, goal, acceptance criteria, non-goals, relevant files and contracts, pre-existing edits, edit boundary, required checks, verification method, and expected evidence.
- Tell the child to execute directly. It must not use this skill to delegate again or start other agents.
- Leave implementation to the child. Do not edit the same checkout while it works. Follow native async completion notifications; do not poll or sleep.
- Route blocking decisions to the user when the task and project instructions do not already answer them. Do not approve new scope on the user's behalf.

If subagent tooling is unavailable before launch, read the persona definition and do the work directly under its rules. State that fallback. If a launch or runtime fails, stop and report the failure and partial work state. Do not silently switch execution methods.

If you are already the delegated implementation child, follow the persona and execute the task directly. Do not launch another agent.

## 4. Test and verify

Use `mise.toml` and `docs/development.md` as the command source. Select the checks that cover the changed seam:

| Change | Checks |
| --- | --- |
| Rust mail core | `mise run test:core`, `mise run lint:core` |
| Rust DTOs or IPC | Regenerate with `mise run gen:ts`; run `mise run check:contract`, core tests, and affected UI/native checks |
| Vue/TypeScript UI | `mise run test:ui`, `mise run typecheck`, `mise run build:web` |
| Tauri shell or bridge | `mise run check:native`, `mise run test:native`, plus affected core/UI checks |
| Cross-cutting work | `mise run check` plus web build and native checks where affected |

Add focused regression tests. Capture before-and-after behavior as required by the persona. Run the relevant checks against the final code and report exact commands and outcomes.

- Use `mise run dev:web` for the synthetic, in-memory browser preview. Use `mise run dev:native` for native fixture verification. Use a background terminal for long-running dev processes.
- Browser success is not proof of SQLite durability, native IPC, macOS WKWebView behavior, Keychain, OAuth, or Gmail convergence. Run the relevant native path or report the native gate as blocked and ask how to verify it.
- Default to synthetic fixtures and fake-provider tests. Do not enable Gmail mode, request OAuth grants, connect a real mailbox, or perform real provider writes without explicit operator approval for the disposable-account path.
- Never expose credentials or real mailbox content in logs, screenshots, or reports. Preserve profile isolation and existing permission boundaries.
- Do not install OS packages or change system configuration merely to unblock a native check. Report missing prerequisites.

## Rust dependency documentation

Check `Cargo.lock` for the exact resolved crate version before looking up its API. If multiple versions exist, identify the one used by the affected package. Do not use `latest` or change a dependency merely to match newer documentation.

- Item index: `https://docs.rs/{crate}/{version}/{crate_underscored}/all.html`
- Specific item: `https://docs.rs/{crate}/{version}/{crate_underscored}/struct.Foo.html` (or `trait.`, `enum.`, `fn.`)
- Source browser: `https://docs.rs/crate/{crate}/{version}/source/`

Use the same version-specific approach for frontend and Tauri documentation, based on `package.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, and `Cargo.lock`.

## 5. Return the result

Review the child's final diff and evidence against the task. Do not equate a successful agent exit with a verified feature. Report:

- What changed and which acceptance criteria it meets.
- Changed file paths.
- Exact checks and results, including failures or skipped gates.
- Before-and-after verification evidence and artifact paths.
- Remaining risks, blockers, and decisions needed.

Do not claim completion when required verification is missing. Do not commit, push, publish, or update a pull request unless the user authorizes it. Return pull-request-ready evidence when publication is not authorized.

content.text:
The account, connection and first-run pass is done, and the PR is open at https://github.com/BbrSofiane/email-os/pull/34. `pnpm test` passes (1024 passed, 33 skipped), and `pnpm typecheck` and `pnpm build` are clean. I did not run any Rust checks because no Rust code changed.

The critique is at `.impeccable/critique/2026-11-08T14-30-00Z__account-connection-first-run.md`. I wrote it before any code and appended the results after. I then had the `persona-feature-engineer` agent implement it test-first.

## What changed
1. **False empty state (P0), fixed.** In Gmail mode, the plain Inbox now shows a line based on connection and sync state, each with an inline action. For example: "Not connected. Connect Gmail", "Sign-in expired. Sign in again", "Syncing first mail… N cached.", "Sync failed: <reason> Retry".
   - The "No conversations are currently in the inbox…" text now appears only when the account is connected, fully synced and empty.
   - In read-only Gmail it now says "No conversations in the cached inbox." instead of promising recovery from Activity. Activity can't restore mail there, so the old sentence was also false.
2. **Header status note.** One `account-status-note` sits in the existing header note slot. It covers not connected, sign-in expired, finish sign-in, syncing, sync failed and offline. The read-only hint steps aside only while a connection problem is showing.
3. **Account drawer.**
   - The bordered card is gone, replaced by four sections: Connection, Sync, Permissions, Session.
   - Disconnect is now a two-step inline confirm, and the warning appears only when you ask.
   - Retry sits next to the sync error.
   - The permanent "Disposable test account" note is removed.
   - During a permission upgrade the drawer says "Finish sign-in in your browser", and "Cancel permission request" is the main button.
4. **Provider mail drawer.**
   - It uses shared styles instead of bare elements.
   - Errors are plain sentences instead of raw `network_unavailable`.
   - A loading line appears before the list.
   - j/k and the arrow keys move between rows, Enter opens, and Escape steps back one level at a time.
5. **Keys.** "Connect Gmail" (or "Sign in again") and "Sync now" are palette commands that appear only while they can run. `g a` goes to Account, using the existing g-chord.
6. **Copy.** "Determining account mode…" is now "Loading account…". Plurals are correct, the default error is "Unknown error.", and the workspace banner is shorter.
7. **Docs.** `DESIGN.md` has a new gap 18 and corrections to gaps 1 and 10. `docs/development.md` and `docs/ux-03-command-discovery.md` are updated.

## Findings I rejected or corrected
- **Reachability (#2) was partly wrong.** The Account entry already exists in the rail and palette whenever the status says Gmail mode, including with no account. The real gap was that nothing pointed to it, and the empty state and header note now do. I only added a test.
- **"Reading works; actions off" (#3) would be false.** Action availability depends only on mailbox-action permission, never on connection, so with an expired sign-in actions still run and fail at Google. The note says only that cached mail stays readable. "Offline" appears only for a `network_unavailable` sync error.
- **"Connecting to your mailbox…" (#6) was not used.** At that point the app is reading local status and nothing is connecting.
- **Switch-button shortcut hint (#6) has no shortcut to show.** Switching accounts is palette-only, so the button's title says "also in Commands".

## Existing tests I changed
Existing assertions changed only where the screen changed on purpose:
- Disconnect now needs a confirm click.
- The disposable note is gone.
- A few labels changed: "Not connected", "Sign-in expired", "permission request pending".
- Provider mail now takes one more Escape to leave.

## Not verified
- Nothing was rendered, because there's no Chrome on this VM. Header-note truncation at narrow widths, drawer spacing and contrast come from the code and design tokens only.
- Screen-reader behaviour is reasoned from the markup, not heard.
- No real Google OAuth, Gmail sync, native offline behaviour or macOS Keychain was exercised. Everything ran against the synthetic in-memory fake.
- Existing limit, now written into `DESIGN.md`: while a connect call is in flight, Cancel sign-in is unavailable. A browser sign-in that never finishes can't be cancelled from the UI.

## Added beyond your list
The agent added three small things you didn't list: an "Account" palette group, a sync glyph in `CommandGlyph.vue`, and an "Initial sync has not finished." line in the drawer. I did not touch the four drawer panels or the reader, compose, search or selection code.

This skill gives you the tools and permission to make design that earns the name out-of-distribution craft. Work as an award-winning design director would: production-grade code, a clear POV, a deep grasp of what the client and its users need, and exceptional craft.

Core principles:
- Finish the job. No hedging, no shortcuts: the deliverable is complete, except assets the user must provide.
- Scale ambition to the surface's mode (see Modes). Persuade and Experience get full commitment: bold, distinct work with a point of view. On Operate and Read, ambition shows as precision and restraint, and patterns the visitor already knows earn their place.
- Verify by looking at the rendered result at the sizes it ships at, and batch the checks: fix what one look shows before looking again, rather than screenshotting after every tweak.

## How to design

- **The brief wins.** Honor pinned aesthetics, eras, materials, fonts, and palettes even when they conflict with a saturated-pattern warning. Redirecting a clear brief toward your taste is failure.
- **Refinement preserves; redesign replaces.** Refinement keeps the incumbent identity, behavior, copy, and everything outside scope. Ask before replacing factual copy or adding claims. Redesign keeps product truth, content, function, native affordances, and constraints, but treats the old look as evidence and anti-reference; choose a replacement world in new-work and replace DESIGN.md. Never split the difference into polish on the discarded look.
- **Loaded symbols stay out of the decoration.** A subject's world does not license emblems tied to militarism, supremacy, or hate movements as motifs, badges, or ornament, such as the Rising Sun flag's rays, the Confederate battle flag, or Nazi-era insignia and their stylised variants; reach for that world's neutral forms instead. Content that documents such a symbol as fact stays as it is.
- **Visual authority is evidence, not a filename.** Missing DESIGN.md alone does not make a project greenfield; new-work decides whether to preserve, expand, or replace the incumbent world.

## Modes

The mode names what the visitor's success looks like on this surface.

- **Persuade:** the visitor decides and acts; design is the product. Landing pages, marketing, campaigns, pricing. Earn attention and action. Ship real imagery when the brief needs it; follow the committed world, not category habit.
- **Operate:** the visitor completes a task. App UI, dashboards, editors, admin, settings, tools. Scanability, consistency, native expectations, and the real usage scene outrank expression. Brand lives in precise details.
- **Read:** the visitor understands something. Docs, articles, guides, help, changelogs. Structure for comprehension, then make the reading experience worth staying in.
- **Experience:** the visitor is inside the work itself. Portfolios, galleries, showcases. Let the artifact lead from the first viewport; the interface recedes.

Choose the mode from the requested surface, not the product, and persist it only in that surface brief. A tool's landing page is still Persuade; a fashion house's documentation is still Read; a docs index is Read, not Persuade. # PRODUCT.md

# Product

## Register

product

## Users

Initially a single person: the author, dogfooding a single-account desktop client (macOS first) against their own Gmail inbox in focused, keyboard-first sessions. They move through a high volume of mail quickly, want to reach "done" on each conversation, and need to trust that every action (archive, bulk processing, undo, send) did exactly what it claimed. The provider's own client remains the fallback.

Longer term: technically capable people who want to compose their own email workflow (custom views, triage signals, commands, automations), manually or with an agent, without rebuilding sync, credentials, or send safety.

The primary task on most screens is triage: scan the list, open a conversation, decide, act, move on.

## Product Purpose

A composable email client: a trusted mail engine (sync, safe rendering, credentials, action execution) with replaceable signals, views, commands, and workflows on top. It ships an opinionated reference experience, a compact Superhuman-style browsing and keyboard flow, rather than a blank toolkit.

The near-term goal is a complete, trustworthy inbox-processing session. Strategic scope is set by `docs/adr/0001-single-account-desktop-email-client.md` and `superhuman-email-browsing-ux-spec.md`; this file does not expand it.

Success looks like: the author processes their inbox faster and with more confidence than in their previous client, and every automated or bulk action is previewable, reported honestly (including partial success and "outcome unknown"), and undoable where undo is real.

## Brand Personality

**Focused, precise, trustworthy.**

- **Focused:** the interface recedes so the mail and the next decision are what's on screen. Dense, quiet, few competing elements.
- **Precise:** exact states, exact counts, exact wording. No vague "something went wrong", no rounded-off truth about what happened.
- **Trustworthy:** the client never overstates what it did. Pending, failed, partial, and ambiguous outcomes are visible and distinct. Automation shows its work before it acts.

Voice is terse and factual: short labels, plain verbs, no exclamation marks, no cheerleading.

## Anti-references

- **Gmail-web clutter:** toolbars of rarely-used icons, chrome competing with content, permanent competing panels.
- **"AI magic" email products:** AI destinations, sparkle icons, generated summaries presented as fact, fabricated contact enrichment, automation that acts without a preview.
- **Superhuman feature-parity clone:** Superhuman is the visual and interaction reference for browsing (layout, density, type, keyboard feel), and close look parity there is a goal. Features and workflows are our own; don't import Superhuman's product scope or claim verified behavioral parity.
- **Generic SaaS dashboard aesthetics:** card stacks and grids, gradient heroes, oversized rounded panels, decorative illustration or motion.
- **Optimistic UI that lies:** "Done" before the provider confirmed, silent retries of ambiguous sends, dead controls that look actionable.

## Design Principles

1. **Honest state over smooth feel.** When speed and truthfulness conflict, show the truth. Every action has a visible pending, success, partial, failed, or unknown state. Show evidence and coverage, including unknown and retained facts.
2. **Keyboard first, mouse welcome.** Every core triage path is reachable and discoverable from the keyboard; pointer interaction is supported, never required.
3. **Content is the interface.** Chrome stays quiet and compact so the list and the conversation dominate. Add UI only when it earns its space in the triage loop; reuse established commands, navigation and recovery surfaces before adding new ones.
4. **Preview before power.** Bulk actions, automations, and agent-proposed changes show what they will do before they do it, and report exactly what they did after. Focus, bulk selection and message identity stay separate concepts.
5. **Opinionated defaults, replaceable parts.** Ship one strong way of working; design surfaces so views, signals, and commands can be swapped without breaking the core experience.

Standing constraints: ordinary reading stays local and non-mutating; message content renders as safe literal plain text; drafts stay local-only.

## Accessibility & Inclusion

Not a formal priority at this stage; no WCAG conformance target or certification is implied. Keyboard operability and visible focus remain required because they are core to the keyboard-first model. Don't regress behavior that already exists (explicit action labels, editable/IME shortcut protection, reduced-motion alternatives, selection/outcome announcements). The existing desktop/contact breakpoints remain authoritative; no new mobile UI. Revisit if the audience expands beyond the author.

294	### Cognitive Load Assessment
295	
296	Cognitive load is the total mental effort required to use an interface. Overloaded users make mistakes, get frustrated, and leave. This reference helps identify and fix cognitive overload.
297	
298	---
299	
300	#### Three Types of Cognitive Load
301	
302	##### Intrinsic Load: The Task Itself
303	Complexity inherent to what the user is trying to do. You can't eliminate this, but you can structure it.
304	
305	**Manage it by**:
306	- Breaking complex tasks into discrete steps
307	- Providing scaffolding (templates, defaults, examples)
308	- Progressive disclosure: show what's needed now, hide the rest
309	- Grouping related decisions together
310	
311	##### Extraneous Load: Bad Design
312	Mental effort caused by poor design choices. **Eliminate this ruthlessly.** It's pure waste.
313	
314	**Common sources**:
315	- Confusing navigation that requires mental mapping
316	- Unclear labels that force users to guess meaning
317	- Visual clutter competing for attention
318	- Inconsistent patterns that prevent learning
319	- Unnecessary steps between user intent and result
320	
321	##### Germane Load: Learning Effort
322	Mental effort spent building understanding. This is *good* cognitive load; it leads to mastery.
323	
324	**Support it by**:
325	- Progressive disclosure that reveals complexity gradually
326	- Consistent patterns that reward learning
327	- Feedback that confirms correct understanding
328	- Onboarding that teaches through action, not walls of text
329	
330	---
331	
332	#### Cognitive Load Checklist
333	
334	Evaluate the interface against these 8 items:
335	
336	- [ ] **Single focus**: Can the user complete their primary task without distraction from competing elements?
337	- [ ] **Chunking**: Is information presented in digestible groups (≤4 items per group)?
338	- [ ] **Grouping**: Are related items visually grouped together (proximity, borders, shared background)?
339	- [ ] **Visual hierarchy**: Is it immediately clear what's most important on the screen?
340	- [ ] **One thing at a time**: Can the user focus on a single decision before moving to the next?
341	- [ ] **Minimal choices**: Are decisions simplified (≤4 visible options at any decision point)?
342	- [ ] **Working memory**: Does the user need to remember information from a previous screen to act on the current one?
343	- [ ] **Progressive disclosure**: Is complexity revealed only when the user needs it?
344	
345	**Scoring**: Count the failed items. 0–1 failures = low cognitive load (good). 2–3 = moderate (address soon). 4+ = high cognitive load (critical fix needed).
346	
347	---
348	
349	#### The Working Memory Rule
350	
351	**Humans can hold ≤4 items in working memory at once** (Miller's Law revised by Cowan, 2001).
352	
353	At any decision point, count the number of distinct options, actions, or pieces of information a user must simultaneously consider:
354	- **≤4 items**: Within working memory limits, manageable
355	- **5–7 items**: Pushing the boundary; consider grouping or progressive disclosure
356	- **8+ items**: Overloaded; users will skip, misclick, or abandon
357	
358	**Practical applications**:
359	- Action buttons: 1 primary, 1–2 secondary, group the rest in a menu
360	- Navigation menus: ≤5 top-level items (group the rest under clear categories)
361	- Long-form articles: one reading path; gather related links into a single block at the end instead of scattering them mid-flow
362	- Documentation sidebars: ≤4 sibling choices visible per level before grouping kicks in
363	- Portfolio and gallery indexes: one decision per screen (which piece to open), not filter, sort, and tag controls all at once
364	
365	---
366	
367	#### Common Cognitive Load Violations
368	
369	##### 1. The Wall of Options
370	**Problem**: Presenting 10+ choices at once with no hierarchy.
371	**Fix**: Group into categories, highlight recommended, use progressive disclosure.
372	
373	##### 2. The Memory Bridge
374	**Problem**: User must remember info from step 1 to complete step 3.
375	**Fix**: Keep relevant context visible, or repeat it where it's needed.
376	
377	##### 3. The Hidden Navigation
378	**Problem**: User must build a mental map of where things are.
379	**Fix**: Always show current location (breadcrumbs, active states, progress indicators).
380	
381	##### 4. The Jargon Barrier
382	**Problem**: Technical or domain language forces translation effort.
383	**Fix**: Use plain language. If domain terms are unavoidable, define them inline.
384	
385	##### 5. The Visual Noise Floor
386	**Problem**: Every element has the same visual weight; nothing stands out.
387	**Fix**: Establish clear hierarchy: one primary element, 2–3 secondary, everything else muted.
388	
389	##### 6. The Inconsistent Pattern
390	**Problem**: Similar actions work differently in different places.
391	**Fix**: Standardize interaction patterns. Same type of action = same type of UI.
392	
393	##### 7. The Multi-Task Demand
394	**Problem**: Interface requires processing multiple simultaneous inputs (reading + deciding + navigating).
395	**Fix**: Sequence the steps. Let the user do one thing at a time.
396	
397	##### 8. The Context Switch
398	**Problem**: User must jump between screens/tabs/modals to gather info for a single decision.
399	**Fix**: Co-locate the information needed for each decision. Reduce back-and-forth.
400

402	
403	### Heuristics Scoring Guide
404	
405	Score each of Nielsen's 10 Usability Heuristics on a 0–4 scale. Be honest: a 4 means genuinely excellent, not "good enough."
406	
407	#### Nielsen's 10 Heuristics
408	
409	##### 1. Visibility of System Status
410	
411	Keep users informed about what's happening through timely, appropriate feedback.
412	
413	**Check for**:
414	- Loading indicators during async operations
415	- Confirmation of user actions (save, submit, delete)
416	- Progress indicators for multi-step processes
417	- Current location in navigation (breadcrumbs, active states)
418	- Form validation feedback (inline, not just on submit)
419	
420	**Scoring**:
421	| Score | Criteria |
422	|-------|----------|
423	| 0 | No feedback; user is guessing what happened |
424	| 1 | Rare feedback; most actions produce no visible response |
425	| 2 | Partial; some states communicated, major gaps remain |
426	| 3 | Good; most operations give clear feedback, minor gaps |
427	| 4 | Excellent; every action confirms, progress is always visible |
428	
429	##### 2. Match Between System and Real World
430	
431	Speak the user's language. Follow real-world conventions. Information appears in natural, logical order.
432	
433	**Check for**:
434	- Familiar terminology (no unexplained jargon)
435	- Logical information order matching user expectations
436	- Recognizable icons and metaphors
437	- Domain-appropriate language for the target audience
438	- Natural reading flow (left-to-right, top-to-bottom priority)
439	
440	**Scoring**:
441	| Score | Criteria |
442	|-------|----------|
443	| 0 | Pure tech jargon, alien to users |
444	| 1 | Mostly confusing; requires domain expertise to navigate |
445	| 2 | Mixed; some plain language, some jargon leaks through |
446	| 3 | Mostly natural; occasional term needs context |
447	| 4 | Speaks the user's language fluently throughout |
448	
449	##### 3. User Control and Freedom
450	
451	Users need a clear "emergency exit" from unwanted states without extended dialogue.
452	
453	**Check for**:
454	- Undo/redo functionality
455	- Cancel buttons on forms and modals
456	- Clear navigation back to safety (home, previous)
457	- Easy way to clear filters, search, selections
458	- Escape from long or multi-step processes
459	
460	**Scoring**:
461	| Score | Criteria |
462	|-------|----------|
463	| 0 | Users get trapped; no way out without refreshing |
464	| 1 | Difficult exits; must find obscure paths to escape |
465	| 2 | Some exits; main flows have escape, edge cases don't |
466	| 3 | Good control; users can exit and undo most actions |
467	| 4 | Full control; undo, cancel, back, and escape everywhere |
468	
469	##### 4. Consistency and Standards
470	
471	Users shouldn't wonder whether different words, situations, or actions mean the same thing.
472	
473	**Check for**:
474	- Consistent terminology throughout the interface
475	- Same actions produce same results everywhere
476	- Platform conventions followed (standard UI patterns)
477	- Visual consistency (colors, typography, spacing, components)
478	- Consistent interaction patterns (same gesture = same behavior)
479	
480	**Scoring**:
481	| Score | Criteria |
482	|-------|----------|
483	| 0 | Inconsistent everywhere; feels like different products stitched together |
484	| 1 | Many inconsistencies; similar things look/behave differently |
485	| 2 | Partially consistent; main flows match, details diverge |
486	| 3 | Mostly consistent; occasional deviation, nothing confusing |
487	| 4 | Fully consistent; cohesive system, predictable behavior |
488	
489	##### 5. Error Prevention
490	
491	Better than good error messages is a design that prevents problems in the first place.
492	
493	**Check for**:
494	- Confirmation before destructive actions (delete, overwrite)
495	- Constraints preventing invalid input (date pickers, dropdowns)
496	- Smart defaults that reduce errors
497	- Clear labels that prevent misunderstanding
498	- Autosave and draft recovery
499	
500	**Scoring**:
501	| Score | Criteria |
502	|-------|----------|
503	| 0 | Errors easy to make; no guardrails anywhere |
504	| 1 | Few safeguards; some inputs validated, most aren't |
505	| 2 | Partial prevention; common errors caught, edge cases slip |
506	| 3 | Good prevention; most error paths blocked proactively |
507	| 4 | Excellent; errors nearly impossible through smart constraints |
508	
509	##### 6. Recognition Rather Than Recall
510	
511	Minimize memory load. Make objects, actions, and options visible or easily retrievable.
512	
513	**Check for**:
514	- Visible options (not buried in hidden menus)
515	- Contextual help when needed (tooltips, inline hints)
516	- Recent items and history
517	- Autocomplete and suggestions
518	- Labels on icons (not icon-only navigation)
519	
520	**Scoring**:
521	| Score | Criteria |
522	|-------|----------|
523	| 0 | Heavy memorization; users must remember paths and commands |
524	| 1 | Mostly recall; many hidden features, few visible cues |
525	| 2 | Some aids; main actions visible, secondary features hidden |
526	| 3 | Good recognition; most things discoverable, few memory demands |
527	| 4 | Everything discoverable; users never need to memorize |
528	
529	##### 7. Flexibility and Efficiency of Use
530	
531	Accelerators, invisible to novices, speed up expert interaction.
532	
533	**Check for**:
534	- Keyboard shortcuts for common actions
535	- Customizable interface elements
536	- Recent items and favorites
537	- Bulk/batch actions
538	- Power user features that don't complicate the basics
539	
540	**Scoring**:
541	| Score | Criteria |
542	|-------|----------|
543	| 0 | One rigid path; no shortcuts or alternatives |
544	| 1 | Limited flexibility; few alternatives to the main path |
545	| 2 | Some shortcuts; basic keyboard support, limited bulk actions |
546	| 3 | Good accelerators; keyboard nav, some customization |
547	| 4 | Highly flexible; multiple paths, power features, customizable |
548	
549	##### 8. Aesthetic and Minimalist Design
550	
551	Interfaces should not contain irrelevant or rarely needed information. Every element should serve a purpose.
552	
553	**Check for**:
554	- Only necessary information visible at each step
555	- Clear visual hierarchy directing attention
556	- Purposeful use of color and emphasis
557	- No decorative clutter competing for attention
558	- Focused, uncluttered layouts
559	
560	**Scoring**:
561	| Score | Criteria |
562	|-------|----------|
563	| 0 | Overwhelming; everything competes for attention equally |
564	| 1 | Cluttered; too much noise, hard to find what matters |
565	| 2 | Some clutter; main content clear, periphery noisy |
566	| 3 | Mostly clean; focused design, minor visual noise |
567	| 4 | Perfectly minimal; every element earns its pixel |
568	
569	##### 9. Help Users Recognize, Diagnose, and Recover from Errors
570	
571	Error messages should use plain language, precisely indicate the problem, and constructively suggest a solution.
572	
573	**Check for**:
574	- Plain language error messages (no error codes for users)
575	- Specific problem identification ("Email is missing @" not "Invalid input")
576	- Actionable recovery suggestions
577	- Errors displayed near the source of the problem
578	- Non-blocking error handling (don't wipe the form)
579	
580	**Scoring**:
581	| Score | Criteria |
582	|-------|----------|
583	| 0 | Cryptic errors; codes, jargon, or no message at all |
584	| 1 | Vague errors; "Something went wrong" with no guidance |
585	| 2 | Clear but unhelpful; names the problem but not the fix |
586	| 3 | Clear with suggestions; identifies problem and offers next steps |
587	| 4 | Perfect recovery; pinpoints issue, suggests fix, preserves user work |
588	
589	##### 10. Help and Documentation
590	
591	Even if the system is usable without docs, help should be easy to find, task-focused, and concise.
592	
593	**Check for**:
594	- Searchable help or documentation
595	- Contextual help (tooltips, inline hints, guided tours)
596	- Task-focused organization (not feature-organized)
597	- Concise, scannable content
598	- Easy access without leaving current context
599	
600	**Scoring**:
601	| Score | Criteria |
602	|-------|----------|
603	| 0 | No help available anywhere |
604	| 1 | Help exists but hard to find or irrelevant |
605	| 2 | Basic help; FAQ or docs exist, not contextual |
606	| 3 | Good documentation; searchable, mostly task-focused |
607	| 4 | Excellent contextual help; right info at the right moment |

642	### Persona-Based Design Testing
643	
644	Test the interface through the eyes of 5 distinct user archetypes. Each persona exposes different failure modes that a single "design director" perspective would miss.
645	
646	**How to use**: Select 2–3 personas most relevant to the interface being critiqued. Walk through the primary user action as each persona. Report specific red flags, not generic concerns.
647	
648	---
649	
650	#### 1. Impatient Power User: "Alex"
651	
652	**Profile**: Expert with similar products. Expects efficiency, hates hand-holding. Will find shortcuts or leave.
653	
654	**Behaviors**:
655	- Skips all onboarding and instructions
656	- Looks for keyboard shortcuts immediately
657	- Tries to bulk-select, batch-edit, and automate
658	- Gets frustrated by required steps that feel unnecessary
659	- Abandons if anything feels slow or patronizing
660	
661	**Test Questions**:
662	- Can Alex complete the core task in under 60 seconds?
663	- Are there keyboard shortcuts for common actions?
664	- Can onboarding be skipped entirely?
665	- Do modals have keyboard dismiss (Esc)?
666	- Is there a "power user" path (shortcuts, bulk actions)?
667	
668	**Red Flags** (report these specifically):
669	- Forced tutorials or unskippable onboarding
670	- No keyboard navigation for primary actions
671	- Slow animations that can't be skipped
672	- One-item-at-a-time workflows where batch would be natural
673	- Redundant confirmation steps for low-risk actions
674	
675	---
676	
677	#### 2. Confused First-Timer: "Jordan"
678	
679	**Profile**: Never used this type of product. Needs guidance at every step. Will abandon rather than figure it out.
680	
681	**Behaviors**:
682	- Reads all instructions carefully
683	- Hesitates before clicking anything unfamiliar
684	- Looks for help or support constantly
685	- Misunderstands jargon and abbreviations
686	- Takes the most literal interpretation of any label
687	
688	**Test Questions**:
689	- Is the first action obviously clear within 5 seconds?
690	- Are all icons labeled with text?
691	- Is there contextual help at decision points?
692	- Does terminology assume prior knowledge?
693	- Is there a clear "back" or "undo" at every step?
694	
695	**Red Flags** (report these specifically):
696	- Icon-only navigation with no labels
697	- Technical jargon without explanation
698	- No visible help option or guidance
699	- Ambiguous next steps after completing an action
700	- No confirmation that an action succeeded
701	
702	---
703	
704	#### 3. Accessibility-Dependent User: "Sam"
705	
706	**Profile**: Uses screen reader (VoiceOver/NVDA), keyboard-only navigation. May have low vision, motor impairment, or cognitive differences.
707	
708	**Behaviors**:
709	- Tabs through the interface linearly
710	- Relies on ARIA labels and heading structure
711	- Cannot see hover states or visual-only indicators
712	- Needs adequate color contrast (4.5:1 minimum)
713	- May use browser zoom up to 200%
714	
715	**Test Questions**:
716	- Can the entire primary flow be completed keyboard-only?
717	- Are all interactive elements focusable with visible focus indicators?
718	- Do images have meaningful alt text?
719	- Is color contrast WCAG AA compliant (4.5:1 for text)?
720	- Does the screen reader announce state changes (loading, success, errors)?
721	
722	**Red Flags** (report these specifically):
723	- Click-only interactions with no keyboard alternative
724	- Missing or invisible focus indicators
725	- Meaning conveyed by color alone (red = error, green = success)
726	- Unlabeled form fields or buttons
727	- Time-limited actions without extension option
728	- Custom components that break screen reader flow
729	
730	---
731	
732	#### 4. Deliberate Stress Tester: "Riley"
733	
734	**Profile**: Methodical user who pushes interfaces beyond the happy path. Tests edge cases, tries unexpected inputs, and probes for gaps in the experience.
735	
736	**Behaviors**:
737	- Tests edge cases intentionally (empty states, long strings, special characters)
738	- Submits forms with unexpected data (emoji, RTL text, very long values)
739	- Tries to break workflows by navigating backwards, refreshing mid-flow, or opening in multiple tabs
740	- Looks for inconsistencies between what the UI promises and what actually happens
741	- Documents problems methodically
742	
743	**Test Questions**:
744	- What happens at the edges (0 items, 1000 items, very long text)?
745	- Do error states recover gracefully or leave the UI in a broken state?
746	- What happens on refresh mid-workflow? Is state preserved?
747	- Are there features that appear to work but produce broken results?
748	- How does the UI handle unexpected input (emoji, special chars, paste from Excel)?
749	
750	**Red Flags** (report these specifically):
751	- Features that appear to work but silently fail or produce wrong results
752	- Error handling that exposes technical details or leaves UI in a broken state
753	- Empty states that show nothing useful ("No results" with no guidance)
754	- Workflows that lose user data on refresh or navigation
755	- Inconsistent behavior between similar interactions in different parts of the UI
756	
757	---
758	
759	#### 5. Distracted Mobile User: "Casey"
760	
761	**Profile**: Using phone one-handed on the go. Frequently interrupted. Possibly on a slow connection.
762	
763	**Behaviors**:
764	- Uses thumb only; prefers bottom-of-screen actions
765	- Gets interrupted mid-flow and returns later
766	- Switches between apps frequently
767	- Has limited attention span and low patience
768	- Types as little as possible, prefers taps and selections
769	
770	**Test Questions**:
771	- Are primary actions in the thumb zone (bottom half of screen)?
772	- Is state preserved if the user leaves and returns?
773	- Does it work on slow connections (3G)?
774	- Can forms use autocomplete and smart defaults?
775	- Are touch targets at least 44×44pt?
776	
777	**Red Flags** (report these specifically):
778	- Important actions positioned at the top of the screen (unreachable by thumb)
779	- No state persistence; progress lost on tab switch or interruption
780	- Large text inputs required where selection would work
781	- Heavy assets loading on every page (no lazy loading)
782	- Tiny tap targets or targets too close together
783	
784	---
785	
786	#### Selecting Personas
787	
788	Choose personas based on the interface type:
789	
790	| Interface Type | Primary Personas | Why |
791	|---------------|-----------------|-----|
792	| Landing page / marketing | Jordan, Riley, Casey | First impressions, trust, mobile |
793	| Dashboard / admin | Alex, Sam | Power users, accessibility |
794	| E-commerce / checkout | Casey, Riley, Jordan | Mobile, edge cases, clarity |
795	| Onboarding flow | Jordan, Casey | Confusion, interruption |
796	| Data-heavy / analytics | Alex, Sam | Efficiency, keyboard nav |
797	| Form-heavy / wizard | Jordan, Sam, Casey | Clarity, accessibility, mobile |
798	
799	---
800	
801	#### Project-Specific Personas
802	
803	If `CLAUDE.md` contains a `## Design Context` section (generated by `impeccable init`), derive 1–2 additional personas from the audience and brand information:
804	
805	1. Read the target audience description
806	2. Identify the primary user archetype not covered by the 5 predefined personas
807	3. Create a persona following this template:

809	```

812	**Profile**: [2-3 key characteristics derived from Design Context]
813	
814	**Behaviors**: [3-4 specific behaviors based on the described audience]
815	
816	**Red Flags**: [3-4 things that would alienate this specific user type]
817	```
818	
819	Only generate project-specific personas when real Design Context data is available. Don't invent audience details; use the 5 predefined personas when no context exists.
